en: The *Dīpaṅkara-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty:
If one plants even a small amount of wholesome merit in a supreme field of merit, one will experience happiness among humans and devas, and later attain nirvāṇa. This is...
A wise person should diligently cultivate and accumulate wholesome karma with a focused mind.
That which is called a "field of merit" is the Buddha himself.
The radiance of the Buddha’s body is like a mass of molten gold, adorned by his own merits and wisdom.
He has attained the perfect eye, being well able to discern the faculties of sentient beings;
he acts as a lamp of light for the darkness of the world and as a benevolent friend to the ignorant among sentient beings;
he is fully endowed with all virtues, and his fame is heard everywhere.
The Muni, the World-Honored One, is the refuge for all; therefore, when humans and devas cultivate merit with a sincere heart, there are none who do not obtain their reward.
In the past, the city of Rājagṛha was surrounded by five mountains, situated at the innermost point among the five Magadhas.

Within this royal city, the streets and lanes run parallel to one another; the gardens and groves are vast and expansive; the towers and pavilions are majestic and beautiful; the halls and chambers are exquisitely adorned; the high balconies are open and bright, surrounded on all sides by railings.
There was a fine grove and pond, most delightful to behold.
Its waters were pure and clear, with a temperature perfectly balanced between warm and cool; canals branched out and water circulated in eddies, flowing back and forth in mutual interconnection.
The forest trees were dense and majestic, their branches and foliage luxuriant; flowers and fruits grew in profusion, obscuring the sun and moon.

When the wind blew through the flowering grove, it produced a subtle and wondrous fragrance; this scent was so pervasive and sweet that its aroma filled all four quarters, permeating the entirety of Rājagṛha.

All those of superior wisdom who practice the holy life, finding this ground uniquely adorned, give rise to joy and happiness in their hearts, traveling from afar to gather together within it like clouds.

At that time, the lord of this city, King Ajātaśatru, had spread his transformative influence far and wide, drawing all people to him; he ruled the kingdom with the True Dharma, and those who cultivated goodness were numerous. The country was prosperous and the population dense, living in peace, security, and happiness.
At that time, there was a householder in the city whose family was immensely wealthy, with storehouses overflowing with riches like those of Vaiśravaṇa; yet, he had no offspring.
He offered prayers and sacrifices to the gods and spirits, seeking to obtain a son. Before long, his wife perceived she was pregnant, and when ten months were complete, she gave birth to a boy.
This child had planted the causes for merit in his previous lives; on the day of his birth, a great radiance issued from one finger of his hand, illuminating ten *li*.

His parents were filled with joy and immediately gathered his kinsmen and various physiognomists to hold a grand assembly for the purpose of naming him. Because of the light from his finger, he was named Dīpāṅgulika (Lamp-Finger).
When those gathered in the assembly beheld these extraordinary signs, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly named Vāśu, who had recited the four Vedas; he was widely learned, possessed great knowledge, and there was nothing he did not understand.
Seeing that the child’s appearance possessed extraordinary and marvelous features, she smiled and said:
"This child must be either Nārāyaṇa, Śakra Devendra, the Sun Deity, or one of the great virtuous gods who has manifested his birth here."
When the child’s parents heard these words, their joy redoubled; they established a great assembly of almsgiving and practiced merit through charity for seven days and seven nights.

As this news spread by word of mouth, it became known throughout the entire kingdom; everyone said that the elder had given birth to a son of great merit, and the sound of such praise reached the ears of the King.
When the king heard this, he immediately issued an order for the child to be brought before him.
Having received the command, the elder promptly took the boy in his arms and went to the gate of the royal palace.
He encountered the king in the midst of a banquet where various musical performances were being held; as no one was available to announce his arrival, he was unable to proceed forward.

The light from the child’s finger shone through and illuminated the palace grounds; it blazed forth with great brilliance, shining upon the king’s body as well as the palaces and pavilions, so that all miscellaneous objects therein became golden in color.
That light shone everywhere throughout the royal palace, like a great body of water, serene and overflowing.
The king, filled with wonder, asked:
"From where does this light come, suddenly illuminating my palace?"
"Could it be that the World-Honored One wishes to transform sentient beings by coming to our door?
Or could it be that the Great Virtuous Devas, Śakra Devānām-Indra, the Sun Deva, and others have descended here?"
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to look outside the gate.
Having seen him, the messenger returned and informed the king:
"The boy whom Your Majesty summoned earlier is now standing outside the gate."
"This child's hand was upon the foster mother's shoulder; light issued from his fingers and shone through clearly, which is why this radiance exists.
The king commanded his messenger, saying, "Bring the child here at once."
When the king saw him, he was deeply struck by this child’s extraordinary nature; he took the child’s hand in his own and examined the marks upon his body.
Having gazed at him intently, he spoke these words:
“The six heretical teachers claim that there is no cause and no effect, deceiving others with falsehoods.”
If there were no cause and effect, how could this child have possessed such transcendent features since birth, and his fingers such brilliant radiance?
Observing this, one sees that the various non-Buddhist practitioners cause sentient beings to fall headlong into the evil realms.

I know for certain that this child was not miraculously produced by Maheśvara, nor did he come into being spontaneously through the gods; he must have obtained this auspicious retribution due to his past merit. Only then do I realize that the Buddha’s words are truly authentic and not false.
"The Buddha has taught that various karmic conditions adorn the world; yet all sentient beings see these retributions with their own eyes and still do not cultivate merit.
How strange this is!
The king spoke again, saying:
"Even now I am not yet certain whether this radiance from the finger is due to the sun.
If you must verify it, we must wait until midnight.
When evening arrived, he placed the child upon the elephant and proceeded ahead; the King, accompanied by his ministers, entered the park together with him.

When the light from this child’s finger illuminated the deep darkness, it became as bright as day; he could observe the birds, beasts, flowers, and fruits within the garden no differently than by daylight.
Having witnessed this, the king sighed deeply and said:
"How truly wondrous is that which the Buddha has spoken!"

Today, I have conceived great and firm faith in cause and effect; I deeply loathe the extreme folly and delusion of the six teachers, and for this reason, my veneration and respect for the Buddha increase all the more.
Then Jīvaka addressed the king, saying:
"The Buddha has stated in the Sūtras that if one does not perceive karma, stinginess and greed arise;
because one perceives karma, stinginess and greed are forever stilled."

Now, seeing that Dīpaṅkara possesses such meritorious retribution, even if one were in extreme poverty, one should still exhaust all resources to cultivate wholesome deeds; how much more so when one is wealthy and prosperous, yet fails to perform merit?
While these words were being spoken, the night had already turned to dawn; he returned with the lamp-finger to the royal palace.
The king was greatly delighted and bestowed upon him a great quantity of precious jewels before releasing him to return home.
As Dīpaṅkara gradually grew up, his father, the elder, sought a marriage alliance for him, selecting a family of high standing equal to his own and taking a daughter from them as his wife.

The elder was wealthy, his rites and teachings were fully perfected, and his household was harmonious; his assets grew ever more prosperous. Yet prosperity is followed by decline, and union must end in separation.

The elder and his wife both passed away at the same time, just as when the sun reaches the place of setting its radiance vanishes, or as when the sun has risen the moonlight does not appear, or as when fire turns to ash and its blazing flames are forever extinguished. Vigor and beauty are destroyed by disease; the prime of youth is encroached upon by old age; and the cherished life is snatched away by death.
Once his parents had passed away, his livelihood gradually declined.

Having grown up in wealth and luxury, this Lamp-Finger was unacquainted with the family business; he associated with evil companions, indulged his heart and will, and became addicted to wine and sensual pleasures. He spent money without restraint, and as no one managed the accumulated stores in the granaries and treasuries, they diminished like the waning moon when it reaches its fullness.
At that time, according to the custom of that country, there was a great annual assembly held at Mount Pañcāla.
On this occasion, Dīpaṅkara, adorned in sumptuous attire and accompanied by musicians and attendants all elegantly arrayed like those of a king, proceeded to that place of assembly.
When the great assembly at that gathering saw this, there was none who did not admire it with reverence.

At that time, the multitude drank together until they were intoxicated, delighting in joy and pleasure; bells and drums resounded in competition, while strings and songs were performed everywhere. They danced merrily across the courtyards and frolicked in the wilds, the sounds of their entertainment shaking the mountains and filling the valleys.

At that time, after Dīpaṃkara had departed for the assembly, a band of thieves, waiting for an opportunity during his absence, went to his house and plundered his wealth, taking everything they could find.
Dīpa returned home in the evening and saw that his house had been plundered by thieves; nothing remained but wood, stones, bricks, and tiles.
Upon seeing this, he fainted and fell to the ground. Only after bystanders sprinkled him with water did he regain consciousness; filled with grief and weeping, he thought to himself:
"My father, throughout his life, extensively applied skillful means to manage the family estate, laboring tirelessly to accumulate wealth and treasures in the storehouses."
"This was done by my father, who gave birth to and raised this body of mine, hoping that there would be one to whom he could entrust his legacy.
How can it be that I have failed to carry on my father's work, wandering aimlessly and indolent, allowing myself to be deceived and oppressed by others?"
In an instant, my father’s remaining wealth was lost; the storehouses were emptied and the livestock scattered. Looking about at the house and estate, I am left all alone.
The necklaces and garments I wear, as well as my carriage, must be sold to provide food and relieve this urgent distress.
"Once these are all exhausted, what shall we do?
At that moment, the light from his finger also vanished; his wife, loathing and despising him, abandoned him and fled, while his servants ran away and his kinsmen cut off all ties with him.
Those who were once intimate and deeply affectionate with him now become like enemies; seeing his poverty, they fear he will beg from them and instead give rise to resentment.
If even his wife abandons him, how much more so others?
One should know that poverty is comparable to hell; a life of poverty is no different from death.
Having previously been accustomed to wealth and pleasure, one suddenly encounters destitution, losing all support and finding no place to dwell.

The fire of anxiety blazes fiercely, and the poison of grief scorches him; his flower-like complexion has faded, and his haggard countenance becomes ever more apparent. His body is emaciated and frail, wasted away by hunger and thirst; his eyes are sunken deep, and his joints stand out like bones. A thin skin clings to him, with sinews and veins exposed; his hair is disheveled and matted, and his hands and feet are thin and withered. His complexion is ashen white, and his entire body is cracked and split; moreover, he has no clothes, having gathered coarse rags from amidst filth and stitched them together to barely cover his private parts. With his four limbs bared, he leans and lies upon heaps of excrement, lacking even a mat or bedding.

His former relatives and acquaintances saw him but did not recognize him; as he wandered through the alleys begging for alms like a starving crow, he approached his close friends intending to beg for food, but the gatekeepers blocked him and would not let him enter.

Watching for an opportunity, he entered once more and again subjected him to insults and humiliation; when the master of the house came out intending to whip him, he bowed his head and stooped his body, prostrating himself twice to apologize for his offense, yet the master treated him with such contempt that he did not even look back.

Even if they were permitted to enter the house, because they were treated with contempt, no one would speak to them nor provide them with seats; they were given only a meager amount of food and drink, which was tossed into their bowls so that they could not be satiated.
At that time, whenever there were ceremonies for taking a wife, giving birth to a child, or shaving the head within that kingdom, it was the custom to hold a feast.
He went to these gatherings hoping to beg for leftover food; however, because he was held in low esteem, they did not call him to sit, but instead drove him about as a servant.
He continued to search for what he needed and obtained only a small remnant, which he shared with his slave from the same vessel.
He then reflected to himself:
"How strange! How strange!"
"How is it that I, now so poor, lowly, and solitary, have suddenly come to this state?
He thought to himself:
"With my spirit so clouded and my mind's faculties lost today, I do not know whether this is my original form or if I have received another body."
Such bitter suffering as this is unparalleled in the world; it is like a forest tree without flowers, from which the swarms of bees depart;
like grass struck by frost, whose leaves wither and curl up;
or like a dried-up pond, where the wild geese do not roam.
Deer do not frequent a forest that has been scorched by fire;
when the crops in a field have been harvested, no one goes to gather the gleanings.
Today I am impoverished; to speak of my former wealth and happiness is but empty talk—who would be willing to believe it?
The world is vast, yet there is no one who knows me.
Because of my poverty, I have no path to turn toward.
It is like a wilderness consumed by fire, which no person finds pleasant.
Like a withered tree that offers no shade for those seeking refuge;
like a crop struck by hail and frost, cast aside and not harvested;
like the lair of a venomous serpent, from which all people keep their distance.
It is like food mixed with poison, which no one will taste;
it is like an empty tomb, toward which no one approaches;
it is like a foul latrine, overflowing with stench and filth.
I am like a butcher, whom people loathe and despise;
I am like a habitual thief, whom people suspect. It is the same with me:
wherever I go, my actions provoke censure and disdain; whatever I speak of, my words give rise to transgression.
Though one speaks well-reasoned words, others deem them wrong;
though one performs virtuous deeds, others regard them as base.
Though one's actions are swift and nimble, they are again disparaged as frivolous and rash.
If he speaks too softly, they say his words are redundant;
if he offers praise, people call it sycophancy;
yet if he does not offer praise, they again give rise to slander, saying that this poor man never has anything good to say.
Furthermore, if he instructs others, they say he is deceitful and pretends to possess ancient wisdom;
if he speaks extensively, people call him loquacious;
if he remains silent, people say he is concealing his true feelings.
If one speaks straightforwardly, they say it is coarse and harsh;
if one seeks to please others' minds, they say it is sycophantic and crooked;
if one associates with them frequently, they say it is deceptive and delusive.
If one does not associate with them, they further claim one is arrogant and boastful;
if one complies with what they say, they further claim one is deceitfully seeking their favor;
if one does not comply, they further claim one is self-opinionated.
If he bends his will to accommodate them, they revile him as being cold and lowly;
if he does not bend his will, they say that though he is a poor man, he still acts with self-importance.
If he slightly relaxes his self-restraint, they call him foolish and lacking in decorum.
If he restrains himself, they say he is empty, coarse, and deceitful, though appearing upright and firm;
if he is again joyous and unrestrained, they say he is boastful and behaves like a madman;
if he is again sorrowful and distressed, they say he harbors poison within and has never had a joyful heart from the start.
If one hears another’s speech that is incomplete, and provides an explanation for it, they say that such a person’s destiny is to replace wisdom with folly through extreme attachment;
yet if one remains silent, they further say that one is stubborn and ignorant, failing to understand the principles of reality;
or if one engages in slight frivolous discourse, they say that one does not believe in the retribution of sin and merit.
If they seek something, they say they will take it regardless of whether they obtain it, showing no sense of shame;
if they seek nothing, they say that although they do not ask for it now, they hope to gain much later.
If they claim to cite the scriptures, they are further said to be feigning cleverness.
If one’s speech is plain and simple, they are further disparaged as being crude and dull-witted.
If one speaks of public matters based on facts, they are said to be using forced arguments;
if one speaks with integrity in private, they are said to be slanderous and sycophantic.
If he wears new clothes, they further say they were borrowed for mere adornment;
if he wears tattered clothes, they further say they are shabby, worn-out, and miserable.
If he eats much, they further say he is hungry and gluttonous.
If one eats little, they claim it is because their stomach is truly hungry, while falsely pretending to be pure and incorruptible.
If they expound upon the sūtras and śāstras, they claim it is to manifest what they know and to expose the ignorance and shortcomings of others;
if they do not expound upon the sūtras and śāstras, they claim it is because they are foolish and ignorant, fit only to tend cattle.
If one speaks of one's own past deeds to boast of one's achievements and praise oneself;
or if one remains silent and claims that one's family background and resources are meager;
or if one regards every movement, gesture, speech, or posture of the poor as entirely a fault or transgression.

Those who possess wealth and status commit various unrighteous acts without any sense of transgression; their every movement and action finds its own justification. The poor person is like a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse), filled with all manner of terrors;

they are like one afflicted by a terminal illness that is difficult to cure, like being in a desolate wilderness where water and grass are utterly absent, like having fallen into the great ocean and being submerged in a surging torrent. They are like a person whose throat is being squeezed so that no breath can escape; like one with a cataract over the eyes who cannot discern where they are going; like thick filth that is difficult to wash away. Furthermore, they are like an enemy who, though sharing food and clothing, does not abandon malice. They are like a well exposed to summer heat where one loses consciousness upon entering; like sinking into deep mud from which it is impossible to emerge;
or like a mountain torrent rushing down with such force that it sweeps away trees and shatters them. Poverty is likewise thus: fraught with many hardships and difficulties.

Poverty can also destroy youthful vigor, beauty, physical strength, and reputation; it ruins one’s lineage and family standing. It can utterly destroy wisdom, observance of precepts, generosity, shame and remorse, benevolence, righteousness, faithfulness, and courageous resolve.
Furthermore, it gives rise to hunger and cold, resentment and hatred, restlessness and narrow-mindedness, sorrow and bitter anguish, and feelings of reproach and guilt.
Such manifold sufferings arise from poverty; just as a hidden treasure contains many miscellaneous items, within the "treasure" of poverty there are many kinds of physical and mental afflictions.

Now, those who possess wealth and nobility have a majestic virtue, a composed countenance, and a broad-minded disposition; they promote the flourishing of ritual and righteousness, can give rise to wisdom and courage, increase their family estate, maintain harmony and deference among their kin, and have their good reputation heard afar.
Dīpaṅkara reflected:
"I am now so impoverished that there is little in the world to compare with my plight; though I wish to sacrifice my body, I cannot bring myself to end my own life.
By what means shall I provide for my own sustenance?"
He further thought to himself:
"Among the things despised by the people of the world, none surpasses carrying a corpse.
Although this task is evil, it does not entail the karma of suffering in future lives."
"If I were to do it myself, I might encounter the taking of life or perform other unwholesome acts.
For this reason, I request that you do it for me.
At that time, a person who heard these words immediately hired him to carry the corpse.
Dengzhi took him straight by the words, carrying the corpse to the cemetery with the intention of casting it away.
At that moment, the dead man suddenly clutched Dengzhi as tightly as a small child clings to its parents; he gripped him so firmly that Dengzhi could not extricate himself despite his utmost efforts.
The corpse clings to his back like glue, impossible to remove; though he pushes and shoves against it, it will not leave, causing him great and intense terror.
He thinks to himself:
"Today I carry this corpse; where can I possibly live?"
He then went to the village of the caṇḍālas and said, "Who among you can remove this corpse from my back? I shall hire you handsomely.
The caṇḍālas consulted together and exerted all their strength to pull it away, yet it would not budge.
Others who saw him reviled the lamp-bearer, saying,
"What is this madman doing, carrying a corpse into a human village?
They vied with one another to strike and pelt him with sticks and stones.
His body was wounded and torn, and both pain and terror came upon him at once.
Moved by compassion, someone led him toward the city, and they eventually arrived at the city gate.
Having reached the foot of the gate, the gatekeeper blocked his way and struck him, preventing him from approaching the gate.
"What kind of foolish person is this, carrying a corpse intending to enter the city?
Seeing his own body covered with wooden staves and his limbs all broken, he was filled with intense remorse and wailed aloud, saying:
"It was solely for the sake of food that I committed such a despicable act."
Today I have suddenly encountered this great suffering because, out of poverty, I did not choose my work carefully; I performed this lowly labor in the hope of obtaining wages to sustain myself.
"How can I encounter such bitter suffering all over again?
It would be better to die another death than to live with a corpse upon my shoulders.
Thus he spoke, weeping as he did so.
At that time, the gatekeeper felt deep compassion and released him to return home.
Upon arriving at his own empty room, those who had previously lived with him as fellow beggars and paupers saw the corpse upon his back from afar and all fled, abandoning him.
Once they had reached the house, the corpse fell to the ground of its own accord.
At that moment, Dīpāṅgulī was overcome with even greater terror; she fainted and collapsed to the floor, regaining consciousness only after a long time.

She then saw that the fingers of the dead body were made entirely of gold. Although she remained fearful, seeing that it was such fine gold, she stepped forward to examine it and tried cutting it with a knife; it was indeed real gold.
Having obtained the gold, his heart was filled with joy; he then cut off his head, neck, hands, and feet.
As soon as they were thus severed, they immediately grew back again.
In a mere moment, the accumulation of his golden heads, hands, and feet exceeded the height of a man.

It is like a king who, having lost his kingdom, regains his original throne; like a blind man who gains sight and sees clearly; like one who has long yearned for another's daughter and finally obtains her company;
or like a practitioner of dhyāna who suddenly attains the realization of the Way—the lamp, the finger, and the joy are likewise so.

His storehouses of precious treasures became twice as great as before; his majesty, virtue, and reputation surpassed those of former days; and all his kinsmen, friends, wife, children, and servants returned to him.
Dengzhi sighed and said:
"Alas, how strange!
Possessing such great power, he is able to cause worldly people to come to him with such extreme swiftness."
Alas, how strange!
Poverty possesses such great power that it can cause even one's closest kin to abandon me with extreme swiftness.
When I was formerly poor, my long-standing intimate friends and associates severed all ties with me; there was not a single person who would speak to me.
Today all gaze upward with earnest expectation, joining their palms in reverent service.
Even if one’s birth were like that of Śakra, one’s valor like that of Rāma, and one’s wisdom like that of the Teacher of Gods, if one lacks wealth, one possesses no value at all.

Whether rich or poor, regardless of whether they are foolish or wise, all call him a good man; though he actually knows nothing, people regard him as intelligent, and he gains renown for being brave, robust, and virtuous;
even though he is ugly, decrepit, and worn out, young women joyfully frequent his side.
When King Ajātaśatru heard that he had become wealthy again, he immediately dispatched men to seize his treasures.
Those who were seized were all dead men, yet when they were thrown back into the house, they were seen to be pure gold.
Dengzhi, knowing that the king desired this treasure, immediately offered his golden head and hands and feet to the king.
Once the king had received them, he carried them back to the palace.
Thereafter, Dīpaṅkara reflected thus and spoke in verse:
“The five desires are extremely fickle and shifting, Like lightning, venomous snakes, and insects;
Prosperity and pleasure do not endure for long— Thus, one gives rise to a mind of weary revulsion.”
He immediately bestowed precious jewels upon the multitude, left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma, and through diligent cultivation attained arhatship.
Although he had realized the fruit of the Path, this corpse-jewel constantly followed after him.
The bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
“For what causes and conditions does the bhikṣu Dīpāṅgulika have this light from his fingers since birth?
For what causes and conditions does he undergo such poverty?”
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does this śarīra-relic treasure constantly follow him?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Listen with a sincere and attentive mind!"
I shall now explain for you his past karmic conditions.

In ages long past, the bhikṣu Dīpāṅgulika was born into the family of a great elder in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. While he was still a young child, he went out to play in a carriage; when he returned late in the evening, the gates were already closed. He called out loudly for the door to be opened, but no one came to respond.
After a long while, his mother came and opened the door for him; he rebuked her angrily, saying:
"Has the whole family carried off a dead person?
Or have bandits come to plunder us?"
"Why is there no one to open the door for me?
Due to these karmic conditions, he died and fell into hell; as a residual retribution from that time, he was reborn among humans and undergoes this poverty and destitution.
I shall further explain for you the causal conditions regarding the Radiant Finger and the causal conditions regarding the Jewel of the Corpse.
Ninety-one eons ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin.
After that Buddha entered nirvana, the Buddha-dharma remained in the world.
At that time, Dīpa was a great elder whose family was immensely wealthy.
He went to a stupa-temple to pay his respects and prostrate; there he saw that a single finger on a clay image had broken off. He immediately repaired this finger, mending it with gold leaf.
Having finished the restoration, he immediately made this vow:

"By the causal conditions of my merit from making offerings of incense, flowers, and music, and from restoring this image, I vow that through this merit I shall be born among gods and humans, always attaining honor, nobility, wealth, and status."
‘Even if it were lost, may I find it again, so that I may leave the household life within the Buddha’s Dharma and attain the Way.
Because he treated the Buddha’s finger, he obtained the light from that finger and a treasure-heap of corpses;
because of his harsh speech, after emerging from hell, he received the retribution of poverty.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Lamp-Finger, the devas and humans scattered various celestial flowers and performed celestial music as offerings; having completed these, they returned to their celestial palaces.

For this reason, if one plants even a small amount of meritorious karma toward an image, the resulting karmic reward is such that it persists even until nirvana; how much more so for the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata?
One who is able to practice the Buddha-dharma according to its teaching possesses such merit that it is immeasurable.
If one wishes to be born among gods or humans to experience various pleasures, one should listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind.

Because of the causes and conditions of harsh speech, one undergoes the retribution of great suffering; therefore, one should fear all forms of suffering and distance oneself from the unwholesome karma of harsh speech.
Observing this, one should realize that the wealth, nobility, and splendor of all worldly people are not worth coveting, and one should find no delight in the honor and status held by others.
One should know that poverty is a mass of great suffering; wishing to sever poverty, one must not be stingy or greedy.
Therefore, it is said in the sutras:
"Poverty is a most grievous suffering.
(From the *Dīpaṅguli-pratyaya-sūtra*)
